hook: This one is told mostly through an interview and an exploration log with people who keep finding themselves somewhere else. It is a slow, grim piece full of twisted corpses, best read in one sitting with the images in view. Expect a deeply unsettling setting.
whyItMatters: It is a strong example of the exploration-log format, where the reader only gets what the subject says aloud. The Foundation's side of the conversation is as much a part of the horror as the ruined city, which makes it a good read for anyone interested in how the site portrays its own staff. Its illustrated addenda also show how artwork can carry an article's final beat instead of text.
thingsToNotice:
The sensory rules are clever: subjects see and smell the other place while only hearing and feeling the lab, so every observation reaches us through someone talking while walking half blind. What they describe is concrete and awful: mummified people with bones bursting out like extra limbs, a child-sized body with a melted head, corpses fused into cubes, a pilot split in half in a six-winged jet, and a mound of bodies at the pillar's base that the illustrator has to climb through.

Watch the interviewer. He coaxes the volunteer onward with the promise of a cure while the procedures at the top of the file order every affected person killed on confirmation, so the reassurances are hollow from the start. The paintings along the pillar tell a story of their own, ending with people wired to the pillar by lines from their heads, and the subject's realization that the city was bent and played with rather than simply destroyed changes how everything before it reads. At the summit he finds a huge many-armed corpse lying on an unfinished final painting whose subject is redacted in the log and only shown as an attached image.
